query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior in HfNbTaTiZr RHEA is primarily governed by intrinsic lattice distortions induced by temperature‐dependent thermal expansion mismatch that creates internal stresses. These stresses interact with dislocation dynamics and promote subtle nanoscale precipitate evolution, thereby unifying the disparate observations from tensile creep, cold rolling, elastic modulus changes, and aging hardening.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) in its as-cast condition, exhibiting inherent chemical short-range order and local lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Subject duplicate sets of the alloy to controlled thermal cycling and mechanical testing in the key temperature range (600–1250 °C). One set remains unmodified, while the other is compositionalally tuned (e.g., with minor Cr addition) to reduce the thermal expansion mismatch.
generation.conditions: Testing in an inert or controlled atmosphere to minimize oxidation effects; temperature steps spanning from below 600 °C (baseline) through 600–1250 °C, with concomitant measurements of stress–strain response, hardness, and elastic modulus.
generation.structural_mediator: Temperature-dependent internal lattice distortions (and concurrent nanoscale precipitate formation) that modify the dislocation mobility and elastic response.
generation.mechanism: As temperature rises, differential thermal expansion among atomic species induces localized lattice mismatches. These mismatches generate internal stresses that enhance work-hardening and alter the elastic moduli. In parallel, these stresses can also subtly promote or hinder nanoscale precipitate evolution, reconciling the observed aging-induced hardening and the changes during cold deformation and creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: The standard alloy (with higher thermal expansion mismatch) will exhibit increased tensile strength, higher work-hardening rates, and more pronounced shifts in elastic moduli at elevated temperatures compared to the compositionally modified alloy with reduced mismatch. At temperatures below 600 °C, these differences should be minimal.
generation.baseline: The alloy tested at room temperature or in a compositional variant engineered to minimize thermal expansion mismatch, where internal stress contributions are negligible.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be dominant in the temperature range 600–1250 °C. Deviations outside this range (e.g., below 600 °C) should reveal minimal changes, and oxidation should be controlled so that its influence remains secondary.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of thermal expansion mismatch versus other strengthening mechanisms (such as solid-solution hardening or precipitate effects) remain uncertain and require further detailed microstructural and in-situ analyses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: (a) standard composition and (b) modified composition with an additive (such as Cr) intended to reduce thermal expansion mismatch without otherwise altering the microstructure. Subject both sets to identical thermal cycling and mechanical testing (tensile creep, hardness, and in-situ elastic modulus measurements) over the temperature range 600–1250 °C.
measurements: In-situ diffraction (e.g., synchrotron XRD) to measure lattice distortions and internal stresses
Microstructural analysis using TEM to assess precipitate formation and dislocation structures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanical properties (e.g., strength, work-hardening rate, and elastic moduli) and measured internal lattice stress indicators show no significant differences between the standard and modified alloys across the 600–1250 °C range, then the hypothesis that thermal expansion mismatch drives the anomalous behavior is falsified.

The so-called high-entropy alloys based on the refractory elements (refractory high-entropy alloys, RHEAs) are considered as candidates for high-temperature applications [,,,,]. Some of them have high strength at T ≥ 1000 °C and thus can potentially operate at higher temperatures than commercial nickel-based superalloys [,,,,,,,,,]. Some RHEAs are sufficiently ductile at room temperature even in tension [,,,,] and can be cold rolled [,,,]. However, refractory elements and their alloys are generally vulnerable to oxidation. A number of studies focused on oxidation behavior of different RHEAs [,,,,,,,,,,] have demonstrated that some of them possess much better oxidation resistance than conventional refractory alloys; however, the oxidation behavior strongly depended on the alloy composition and testing conditions. Note that the vast majority of the performed research was conducted at temperatures of T ≥ 1000 °C [,,,,,,].
